beats.text: Go and get your electric bill. Right now, before we start, not the envelope, the bill.
Now don't look at what you owe. Everybody looks at what you owe.
Turn it over, second page usually, that column of small gray print where they take the bill apart.
Look at how many lines are on that cage.
You saw $214 and figured you ran the air too hard in July.
That wasn't it, neighbor. Somewhere between $30 and $60 of what's on that page never touched a wire.
On some of those lines you're paying for power. On the rest, you're paying for paperwork.
And it was never your thermostat. Nobody ever sat at a table with you and read this page out loud.
That's the whole trick. That's all it ever was. My grandmother Ruth kept a household ledger from 1929 to 1939.
It's on the table in front of me right now. April 1934.
The power bill. One line. A number of kilowatt hours, a rate, a total.
That's the whole thing. If a second number had ever shown up on that page, she'd have put her coat on, walked down to the office,
and asked a man what it was for. And she'd have taken me with her so I'd learn how it's done.
She wasn't smarter than you. She just got a bill she could read.
So today we read yours. Fourteen charges. And I'll be straight with you first, because I won't promise you something that isn't true.
Six of these you can kill outright. Five you can shrink.
Three you're stuck with, and no phone call on earth will move them.
And here's what costs people the most money. The three you're stuck with are the three everybody spends the whole call arguing about.
So we're going to sort them, and you'll spend your energy in the right place.
We count down from 14. Everyone comes with the why, because in this house, we don't fight a bill we don't understand.
Number one is the biggest by a long way. In one state, this past April, it cost nine companies $50 million in refunds to 278,000
households. Stay with me for that one. Number 14.
The paper bill fee. Kill it. One to three dollars a month for the crime of receiving a piece of paper.
Look for paper statement, billing fee, or convenience charge.
If it's there, switch to email billing and it's gone tonight.
90 seconds online. $36 a year.
That's not life-changing money, and I know it. I put it at 14 on purpose, so you'd see how small they're willing to go.
If a company will charge you $2 for an envelope, ask yourself what else is sitting on that page.
Number 13. The smart meter opt-out fee.
Kill it. Five to $15 a month, plus a setup charge, for a decision you might have made once, years ago,
and never thought about since. When the smart meters came around, a lot of people opted out.
Some had reasons. Most just checked a box on a letter, and that box turned into a monthly charge that's been writing your bill ever since.
Sometimes for 10 years. Look for opt-out, manual read, or non-standard meter.
If you don't remember choosing it, one phone call reverses it.
$180 a year for a box you don't remember checking.
Number 12. The late fee. Shrink it. Two things almost nobody knows.
First, most utilities will waive one late fee a year as a courtesy if you call and ask plainly.
Not argue. Ask. They'll very often say yes.
Second one's better. You can move your due date.
Most utilities will shift your billing cycle so it lands after your payday or your benefit deposit, and it costs nothing.
If you've been getting hit with late fees for years, the problem was never your money.
It was the date. Number 11. The deposit they're still holding.
Kill it. When you opened the account, you may have paid a security deposit.
$100, $200, sometimes more.
In most places, it's supposed to come back after 12 months of on-time payment.
In some places, it's supposed to earn interest while they sit on it.
But here's the part, neighbor. It comes back when you ask.
A refund nobody claims is a refund nobody pays.
If you've been in that house for years and never once seen a deposit come back, that's a phone call this week.
My grandmother's ledger has a whole column for money other people were holding.
One column so it could never be forgotten. That's all a ledger is.
A way of not forgetting. Number 10. The equipment rental.
Kill it. This is the one that makes people angry, and it should.
In a lot of markets, a rental charge rides along on the utility bill.
A water heater, a surge protection plan, a line warranty, $8, $12, $15 a month.
Somebody signed up once. Sometimes it came with the house and the last owner signed up.
And it's been renting you that water heater for 20 years, which means by now you've bought it four or five times over.
Look for rental, protection plan, warranty, or a company name you don't recognize next to a flat monthly figure.
If you don't know what it is, that's exactly why you call.
Number nine. The franchise fee. You're stuck.
First one I can't help you kill, and I'll say so plainly instead of selling you a fix.
Your city charges the utility for the right to run wires over public ground.
The utility passes it straight to you as a percentage.
It isn't the power company's money and they cannot waive it, but it is a percentage, which makes it the only good news in the stuck column.
Every dollar you take off the rest of this bill, this line shrinks by itself.
Number eight. State and local utility tax.
Stuck. Same story. A tax on utility service, passed through, and nobody on that phone can take it off.
I'm giving it its own number for one reason, so you stop spending your energy there.
Most folks who call angry burn the whole call on the taxes and hang up before they reach the lines that could have moved.
Skip these two. Go where the money is. Number seven.
The energy efficiency surcharge. Shrink it.
A small monthly rider. An efficiency charge, a conservation charge, a public benefit fund.
Different name, same line. You can't remove it, but it matters more than its size, and here's why.
That surcharge funds programs you've already paid for and almost certainly never used.
Free home energy audits, free insulation and weather stripping, free LED replacements, rebates on appliances.
You bought all of that, neighbor, every month for years.
Go collect it. Call and ask what your efficiency charge entitles you to.
Almost nobody thinks to ask. Number six. Storm recovery.
Stuck. After a bad storm, a utility spends heavily rebuilding lines, then recovers that money from customers over a stretch of years.
Storm recovery, storm cost, securitization charge.
You can't remove it. It does have an end date, written into the order that created it.
I'm telling you what it is so you can quit wandering. A charge you understand stops costing you sleep even when it doesn't stop costing you money.
Number five. The fuel adjustment. Shrink it.
Fuel adjustment. Power cost recovery. Purchased power adjustment.
Different name in every state, same animal. This is the part of your rate that moves with what it costs to generate the power.
Not fixed, not negotiable, and a big part of why your bill has climbed so hard these last five years.
But because it floats, it rewards you for changing when you use power rather than how much.
Which takes us into number four. Number four. The basic service charge.
Shrink it. The fixed monthly charge you pay before you've used a single kilowatt hour.
Shut everything off for 30 days and it still shows up.
You can't get rid of it, but hardly anybody knows this next part.
The amount changes depending on your rate class and your utility runs several.
Standard residential, time of use, low income, medical, all electric home.
If somebody put you on a rate class in 1998 and nothing's been looked at since, you might be sitting on the wrong one,
which is number three. Number three. The wrong rate class.
Kill it. Biggest one on this list that costs nothing to fix.
Write these words down. Ask your utility this exact question.
What rate class am I on? What else do I qualify for?
And can you compare my last 12 months on each one? They can do it.
The data is right there in front of them. They will not offer it.
Three to ask about by name, a medical baseline rate, if anybody in the home runs medical equipment,
a low income or discount rate, and most states have one and the income limits run higher than people expect.
And time of use against flat rate, because whichever one you're on, the other might fit your household better.
20 to $60 a month for a great many households.
One phone call, nothing to buy. Number two.
Peak pricing. Shrink it. If you're on a time of use rate, the same kilowatt hour costs two or three times more between roughly four and nine in the evening
than it does at any other hour of the day. Same power, same wire, same house.
The clock is the only difference. Dishwasher after nine.
Laundry in the morning. Charge the car overnight.
And if you cook at six, well, you cook at six. That's your life, and I'm not going to sit here and tell you to eat at 10.
My grandmother did her washing Monday mornings, and my whole childhood, I thought that was tradition.
It wasn't. It was rate structure. She was doing the exact thing I'm asking you to do 90 years ago, and nobody had to tell her twice.
Number one. The third party supplier. Kill it.
Here it is. Find the section of your bill marked supply, not delivery supply, and look at the company name printed there.
If it's a company you've never heard of, one that knocked on your door a few years back or called you at dinner promising to save you money,
then you're with a third party supplier, and there's a real chance you're paying well above your utility's own default rate for identical electricity down the identical wire
into the same house. This isn't a theory, and I'm not guessing.
In Connecticut, a state consumer council report found 86% of one utility's third party supply customers paid more than the standard rate,
86%. In New York this past April, regulators made nine affiliated suppliers return roughly $50 million to about 278,000
households. The pattern's always the same. A low rate for two or three months, then it moves, and it keeps moving,
and nobody writes to tell you. Here's how you check, and it takes 30 seconds.
Your bill prints your supply rate in cents per kilowatt hour.
Your utility publishes its own default rate on its website.
Put the two side by side. If yours is higher, you can switch back to the default, and in most states that's free and takes one billing cycle.
Some households find $8 or $10, some find $60, and some find out they've been overpaying for 11 years.
Now, an honest word, because I won't leave you holding a number I can't stand behind.
You will not remove all 14. Nobody does.
Three of them cannot be removed at all, and I told you that at the start instead of the end.
And if you work this whole list and find you're on the right rate, buying from the utility itself, no rentals, no opt-out fee,
then your bill is high because power is expensive right now, and no phone call fixes that.
That's a true answer, and you deserve to have it. But most people are not that household.
Most people have three or four of these sitting on their bill tonight.
When you call, you don't need a speech. You need five questions in this order.
One, what rate class am I on, and what else do I qualify for?
Two, am I on your default supply or a third-party supplier?
Three, is there a rental, a warranty, or an opt-out fee on this account?
Four, are you still holding a deposit for me?
Five, can I move my due date? 12 minutes.
Read them right off the page. You're not arguing with anybody, neighbor.
You're asking a company what it's charging you, and that's the most ordinary question in the world.
Don't do all five tonight though. Do one thing.
Turn the bill over, find the supply section, and read the company name, just the name.
That's the whole task, because if it's a name you don't recognize, that's number one on this list, and you'll want to make that call in the morning.
Tell me in the comments what you found on that page, what state you're in, and the strangest line item on your bill.
I read every one, and the strange ones are how I find the next 14.
